questions.prompt: How is an indexer declared and used?
options: With a name like `Item`, and called as `collection.Item(0)`
With `this[parameterType index]`; it has no name and is used with `[]` on the object
With the `indexer` keyword, and it can only have a `get` accessor
As a static method that returns an array
questions.explanation: An indexer is declared with `this[parameterType index]`, can have `get` and/or `set` accessors, can be overloaded, and has no name: you use `[]` directly on the object.

questions.prompt: Why can't you pass a property as a `ref` or `out` argument?
options: Because properties are always read-only
Because properties are stored on the stack
Because a property is really `get_`/`set_` methods, so there is no storage location to pass
Because `ref` and `out` only work with static members
questions.explanation: Under the hood a property is two methods, `get_PropertyName()` and `set_PropertyName(value)`. `ref` and `out` need the actual storage location of a variable, which a property does not expose.

questions.prompt: A property is declared `public string Name { get; init; }`. When can `Name` be set?
options: Only during object initialization, such as `new Student { Name = "Aman" }`
At any time, like a normal `set`
Never; `init` makes it a compile-time constant
Only inside a static constructor
questions.explanation: Init-only properties (C# 9+) can be set at object initialization only; a later assignment like `s.Name = "Raj"` is not allowed.

questions.prompt: `Middle : Base` declares `public sealed override int Value { get; set; }`. What does `sealed` mean here?
options: `Value` can no longer be read from outside `Middle`
`Middle` itself can no longer be inherited
`Value` becomes a static property
A class derived from `Middle` cannot override `Value` again
questions.explanation: On a property, `sealed` prevents further derived classes from overriding an already overridden property, so classes derived from `Middle` cannot override `Value`.

questions.prompt: `Employee` is an abstract class that implements `IWorker`, which declares `void Work();`. Does `Employee` have to provide a body for `Work()`?
options: Yes; every class must implement all interface members itself
No; it can declare `public abstract void Work();` and let a concrete derived class implement it
No; interface members are implemented automatically
Yes, unless `Work()` is marked `static`
questions.explanation: An abstract class may implement an interface member, declare it abstract, or defer it to a later derived class; a concrete class such as `Developer` must implement it.
